title: YOU SAY YOU’RE WAITING ON GOD… BUT WHAT IF GOD IS WAITING FOR YOU TO OBEY?
paragraphs: YOU SAY YOU’RE WAITING ON GOD… BUT WHAT IF GOD IS WAITING FOR YOU TO OBEY?
The Most Dangerous Delay in Your Christian Life May Be the One You’ve Learned to Call “Faith.”
What if the door you keep begging God to open is already open… but you are standing outside, asking Him for another sign because walking through it would cost you something?
Read that again.
Because there is a kind of waiting that honors God.
And there is a kind of waiting that sounds spiritual, looks patient, quotes Scripture, and even comes wrapped in prayer… but underneath it is a frightened heart refusing to surrender.
And the terrifying part?
You can spend years calling it faith when it is actually disobedience.
You pray, “Lord, show me what to do.”
But He already showed you.
You pray, “Lord, give me confirmation.”
But His Word has already spoken.
You pray, “Lord, change my circumstances.”
But perhaps the first thing He is calling you to surrender is the very thing you keep defending.
You are waiting for peace before forgiving someone.
Waiting for confidence before serving.
Waiting for financial security before becoming generous.
Waiting for the perfect moment to confess what you have hidden.
Waiting for your feelings to change before leaving a relationship that keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Waiting until you feel worthy before returning to God.
And all the while, you keep whispering…
“I'm just waiting on the Lord.”
But what if the question is no longer whether God has spoken?
What if the question is whether you are willing to obey what He has already said?
Because sometimes the hardest part of following Jesus is not discovering His will.
It is surrendering our own.
And before this message is over, there is something you need to understand about the difference between waiting in faith and hiding behind waiting.
It might change the way you pray tonight.
It might also change what you do tomorrow morning.
There was a man lying near a pool in Jerusalem.
Not for a few days.
Not for a few months.
For thirty-eight years, he had lived with his disability.
Thirty-eight years of watching other people move while he remained where he was.
Thirty-eight years of disappointment.
Thirty-eight years of a life he probably never imagined would turn out this way.
John 5:6 records a question Jesus asked him:
“Wilt thou be made whole?” (KJV)
In the Greek text, Jesus asks:
θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι;
Theleis hygiēs genesthai?
“Do you want to become well?”
Think about that.
Jesus knew the man's condition. He knew how long he had suffered. He was not asking because He lacked information.
He was confronting the man with a personal question in the middle of a painful reality.
And the man's answer was heartbreaking.
“Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool…” (John 5:7, KJV).
He explained his circumstances.
He explained the obstacle.
He explained why nothing had changed.
And to be fair, his suffering was real.
His limitations were real.
His need for help was real.
Jesus did not mock him for any of it.
But then Jesus spoke:
“Rise, take up thy bed, and walk.” (John 5:8, KJV).
And immediately the man was made well.
Notice something important.
The man's healing did not come because he finally manufactured enough willpower to change his condition. It came through the authority and power of Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because the Gospel is not a motivational speech telling helpless people to save themselves.
It is the announcement that the Savior has come to do what sinners cannot accomplish on their own.
But when Christ commanded the man to rise, His word called for a response.
And this is where the story begins to search our hearts.
Not because every sickness is caused by disobedience.
Not because every unanswered prayer means we have failed God.
Not because every believer who is still waiting has somehow refused to move.
Those conclusions would distort Scripture and wound people whom Jesus loves.
The question is much more personal.
Where has Jesus already made your responsibility clear, but you keep asking Him to make obedience easier?
Maybe you know exactly where.
That apology you have been rehearsing but never offering.
That secret sin you keep promising to abandon after one more time.
That person you need to stop manipulating.
That dishonest practice you have convinced yourself is necessary to survive.
That bitterness you have nurtured so long it now feels like part of your identity.
That conversation with your spouse you keep postponing because honesty might expose what has been dying between you.
That act of repentance you keep delaying because you are afraid of what it will cost.
And maybe nobody knows.
Not your family.
Not your pastor.
Not the people who see you sharing Bible verses online.
They see the Christian you present to the world.
But God sees the battle you fight when the room goes quiet.
He sees the deleted messages.
The hidden compromises.
The tears you wipe away before anyone walks in.
The excuses you have repeated so many times that you almost believe them.
And still, in His mercy, He calls you.
Not to humiliate you.
But to bring you into the light.
Because the God who exposes sin is also the God who offers forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
Now consider another man.
His name was Jonah.
God told him to go to Nineveh.
The instruction was clear.
But Jonah went in the opposite direction.
He boarded a ship headed toward Tarshish, fleeing from the mission God had given him.
And here is something we need to remember.
Jonah was not confused about God's instruction.
He resisted it.
Later, Jonah revealed that he knew God was gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in lovingkindness (Jonah 4:2).
His problem was not a lack of information about God's character.
His problem was that he did not want God's mercy extended to people he despised.
That is a frightening possibility.
You can know Scripture.
You can understand theology.
You can recognize God's goodness.
And still resist what His goodness requires of you.
Some people are not waiting because God's will is unclear.
They are waiting because obedience would threaten something they are determined to keep.
Their pride.
Their comfort.
Their reputation.
Their control.
Their resentment.
Their preferred future.
And that is why the words of James 4:17 should make us examine ourselves:
“Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.” (KJV).
The Greek expression translated “to do good” includes:
καλὸν ποιεῖν
Kalon poiein.
To do what is good.
James is not teaching that Christians must act impulsively whenever they feel guilty or pressured.
He is confronting the moral responsibility of someone who recognizes what is right and knowingly refuses to do it.
There is a difference between not knowing what God requires and knowing but refusing.
And that difference matters.
Because spiritual language can become a hiding place for an unwilling heart.
“I’m praying about it.”
Sometimes that means genuine dependence.
Sometimes it means we are hoping God will eventually give us permission to do what we already want.
“I’m waiting for peace.”
Sometimes that means patiently seeking wisdom.
Sometimes it means we have confused peace with the absence of discomfort.
“I’m waiting for the right time.”
Sometimes that is prudent.
Sometimes it means we are hoping the cost of obedience will disappear.
But obedience does not always feel comfortable.
Ask Abraham.
God called him to leave his homeland without revealing every detail of the journey ahead (Genesis 12:1–4; Hebrews 11:8).
Abraham did not possess a complete map.
He had the promise of a faithful God.
Ask Peter.
After a night of unsuccessful fishing, Jesus instructed him to let down the nets.
Peter answered:
“Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.” (Luke 5:5, KJV).
Nevertheless, at Thy word.
Not because the circumstances looked promising.
Not because Peter suddenly understood everything.
But because Jesus had spoken.
There is something deeply beautiful about that kind of faith.
Faith that says, “Lord, I am afraid, but I trust You.”
Faith that says, “I do not know how this will turn out, but I will not knowingly disobey You.”
Faith that says, “My feelings are loud, but Your Word is greater.”
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have been avoiding.
Not “Lord, give me another sign.”
But “Lord, give me a willing heart.”
Because obedience is not always a dramatic moment at an altar.
Sometimes it is deleting the number.
Sometimes it is telling the truth.
Sometimes it is admitting you were wrong.
Sometimes it is returning money that was never yours.
Sometimes it is asking for help with an addiction you have hidden for years.
Sometimes it is opening the Bible after months of spiritual neglect.
Sometimes it is choosing not to retaliate against someone who wounded you.
Sometimes it is seeking wise counsel instead of making another reckless decision.
Sometimes it is simply doing the next faithful thing that Scripture has already made clear.
And sometimes…
Obedience means waiting.
Yes. Waiting.
Because not every delay is disobedience.
David was anointed king long before he sat on Israel's throne.
He endured danger, uncertainty, and years of hardship.
And when he had opportunities to seize power by killing Saul, he refused to take the throne through wrongdoing (1 Samuel 24; 26).
David's waiting was not necessarily avoidance.
At those moments, refusing to act wickedly was itself an act of obedience.
That is why we must never turn this message into a weapon against people who are genuinely waiting on God.
A woman praying for healing is not automatically disobedient because she remains sick.
A couple longing for a child is not spiritually defective because the nursery is still empty.
A believer seeking employment is not necessarily lazy because a door has not opened.
A person recovering from trauma is not resisting God simply because healing takes time.
And someone facing a complicated decision may genuinely need counsel, prayer, and patience.
Scripture says:
“Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD.” (Psalm 27:14, KJV).
In Hebrew, the command includes:
קַוֵּה אֶל־יְהוָה
Qavveh el-YHWH.
“Wait for the LORD.”
The Hebrew verb qavah carries the sense of waiting with expectation and hope.
Biblical waiting is not necessarily inactivity.
It is trusting God's timing while remaining faithful to what He has already revealed.
And that is the distinction.
Faithful waiting refuses to run ahead of God. Disobedient delay refuses to follow where God has already led.
One is trust.
The other may be fear dressed in religious clothing.
And only an honest heart before God can begin to discern the difference.
But there is another part of this message that may be harder to hear.
What if your greatest fear is not that God will remain silent?
What if your greatest fear is that He will answer clearly… and ask you to surrender the one thing you have built your life around?
That relationship.
That ambition.
That image of yourself.
That need to be admired.
That secret pleasure.
That resentment you believe you have earned the right to carry.
What if the thing you are most afraid to release is the very thing keeping your heart divided?
Remember the rich young ruler.
He approached Jesus with a serious question about eternal life.
He had moral accomplishments.
He had religious knowledge.
He had wealth.
But Jesus exposed the particular attachment that held his heart.
Christ called him to sell what he possessed, give to the poor, and follow Him (Mark 10:17–22).
And the young man walked away grieving.
Not because Jesus lacked love for him.
Mark 10:21 explicitly tells us that Jesus loved him.
That detail is devastating.
Jesus loved him.
And Jesus still called him to costly surrender.
Because genuine love does not always tell us what we want to hear.
Sometimes love confronts the very thing destroying us.
And perhaps that is why this message is uncomfortable.
Because somewhere between our worship songs and our daily decisions, we have begun treating surrender as optional.
We want Jesus as Savior.
But we struggle with Jesus as Lord.
We want forgiveness without confession.
Freedom without repentance.
Transformation without surrender.
A cross that comforts us, but never confronts us.
Yet Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23, KJV).
In Greek, the phrase translated “let him deny himself” is:
ἀρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν
Arnēsasthō heauton.
It expresses the call to deny oneself.
Not to despise one's God-given worth.
Not to tolerate abuse.
Not to abandon necessary rest, wisdom, or healthy boundaries.
But to renounce the claim that our own desires, ambitions, and preferences have the final authority over our lives.
Jesus does.
And following Him is not a negotiation in which we retain the right to disobey whenever His commands become inconvenient.
But listen carefully.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because if this article ended with “Try harder. Obey better. Stop failing,” it would leave us crushed beneath a burden we cannot carry by ourselves.
And that is not the good news of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel begins with the truth that we are sinners who cannot earn our salvation.
We have not merely made occasional mistakes.
We have rebelled against the holy God who created us.
And no amount of religious performance can erase that guilt.
But God did not leave us without hope.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered our broken world.
He obeyed the Father perfectly.
He loved without corruption.
He spoke truth without compromise.
He bore our sins upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day.
The salvation we could never purchase was accomplished through Him.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV).
Do not miss the next verse.
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works…” (Ephesians 2:10, KJV).
We are not saved because we obey.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ, and that grace begins transforming how we live.
Obedience is not the price of God's acceptance.
It is a fruit of the new life He gives.
That changes everything.
Because now obedience is no longer a desperate attempt to make God love us.
It becomes a response to the Savior who loved us first.
And when we fail, we do not have to run farther into darkness.
We can return to Him in repentance.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV).
There is grace for the person who delayed.
Grace for the person who ran.
Grace for the person who compromised.
Grace for the person who pretended.
Grace for the person who knew better and still chose wrongly.
Not grace that excuses continued rebellion.
Grace that calls us out of it.
Grace that restores.
Grace that teaches.
Grace that changes us from the inside out.
Look at Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
Then, under pressure, he denied knowing Him three times.
Imagine the shame.
The sound of the rooster.
The crushing realization of what he had done.
Peter had failed the very Lord he loved.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with responsibility to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The man who had denied Christ became a bold witness to Christ.
That is not because betrayal was insignificant.
It is because the mercy of the risen Savior was greater than Peter's failure.
And maybe someone reading this needs that truth more than another warning.
You have delayed obedience for so long that you wonder whether God could still use you.
You have made promises and broken them.
You have repented, struggled, fallen, and cried over the same weakness.
You have watched other believers grow while you feel trapped in the same spiritual battle.
And now shame whispers, “You have wasted too much time.”
But shame is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
And the same Lord who confronted Peter also restored him.
Your past matters.
Your choices have consequences.
Some damage requires confession, restitution, accountability, and a long process of rebuilding trust.
Grace does not erase every earthly consequence.
But in Christ, your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by offering cheap forgiveness without repentance.
But by redeeming sinners through His blood and transforming lives through His Spirit.
So perhaps tonight you do not need another dramatic spiritual experience.
Perhaps you need to kneel beside your bed, with no audience, no religious performance, and no carefully polished words, and tell God the truth.
“Father, I have been calling it waiting, but I know there are things You have already commanded me to do.
I have been afraid.
I have been stubborn.
I have protected my comfort more than I have pursued Your will.
I have asked for confirmation when what I really wanted was permission to delay.
Forgive me.
Cleanse me through Jesus Christ.
Give me the courage to obey You, the humility to seek counsel where I need wisdom, and the patience to wait where You have not yet opened the way.
I do not want to run ahead of You.
But I do not want to keep running away from You either.
Teach me to follow Jesus, even when obedience costs me something.
Not to earn Your love, but because Your love has reached me.
In Jesus' name, amen.”
And after that prayer?
Do not mistake emotion for transformation.
Tears can be sincere.
Conviction can be powerful.
But when God has made the next faithful step clear, repentance calls us to respond.
Maybe you need to send that apology.
Maybe you need to confess the truth.
Maybe you need to end a sinful compromise.
Maybe you need to reconcile with someone, where it is safe and appropriate.
Maybe you need to ask your pastor or a mature Christian for help.
Maybe you need to stop waiting for the feeling of readiness and begin with the strength God provides.
Or maybe you need to remain where God has placed you, trusting Him without taking shortcuts that violate His Word.
Whatever the situation, do not let someone else's urgency become your substitute for God's guidance.
Test what you believe God is asking against Scripture.
Seek wise counsel.
Pray honestly.
And where His Word is clear, do not spend another year trying to negotiate away the cost of following Him.
Because time is precious.
And the life you have been given is not meant to be spent endlessly postponing faithfulness.
There are people who need your forgiveness.
People who need your honesty.
People who need the encouragement you have been withholding.
People who may hear the Gospel because you finally stop hiding your faith.
And there may be someone reading these very words who has almost given up on Jesus.
Someone who thinks their repeated failures have placed them beyond His mercy.
Someone who is waiting for proof that God has not abandoned them.
If that is you, hear this.
Christ still calls sinners to come to Him.
His cross is sufficient.
His resurrection is real.
His grace is not exhausted.
And today is a good day to turn toward Him.
Not because you have finally become strong enough.
But because He is mighty to save.
Someone else may need to know that surrender is not the end of hope.
There is room here for people who are growing, questioning, grieving, repenting, learning, and discovering the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.

The Gospel Warrior mission is to keep sharing biblical truth, Christ-centered encouragement, discipleship resources, and messages that call people beyond religious appearances into genuine faith in Jesus.
These resources are intended to nourish faith, encourage spiritual maturity, and help people discover the riches of God's Word.
But we want to be clear about something that matters deeply.
Your obedience to Jesus cannot be measured by a payment.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
And your tithe, giving, and stewardship should be directed by biblical conviction, wise discernment, and your responsibilities before the Lord.
Scripture says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).
The Greek word translated “of necessity” is ἀνάγκης (anankēs), expressing compulsion or constraint.
God-honoring generosity should never be manufactured through guilt or spiritual pressure.
It is the opportunity to participate in a mission centered on Jesus Christ.
A mission that proclaims repentance without abandoning grace.
That speaks about sin without forgetting the cross.
That offers encouragement without watering down truth.
That reminds broken people that redemption is possible through the risen Savior.
It is about His glory.
His truth.
His grace.
His people.
And the salvation that is found in Him alone.
Before you leave, I want to return to the question we began with.
You say you are waiting on God.
And perhaps you truly are.
If He has called you to wait, then wait with faith. Wait with courage. Wait without surrendering to despair.
But if His Word has already made your next step clear…
If you know the truth you have been avoiding…
If you know the sin you need to confess…
If you know the compromise you need to abandon…
If you know the person you need to forgive…
If you know the responsibility you keep postponing…
Then do not confuse another day of delay with another day of devotion.
You may not know what tomorrow will bring.
You may not know how every consequence will unfold.
You may not know whether the road will become easier.
But you can know the One who calls you.
The One who went to the cross.
The One who conquered the grave.
The One who restores the repentant.
The One who gives His Spirit to those who belong to Him.
And the One whose grace is sufficient for the next faithful step.
So tonight, perhaps the prayer is no longer, “Lord, why haven't You moved?”
Perhaps it is…
“Lord, where have I refused to follow?”
And when His Word shows you the answer, do not run from the light.
Run to Jesus.

Because the saddest thing would not be discovering that you waited a long time for God—it would be realizing that, while calling it waiting, you spent years running from the very Savior who was calling you to follow Him.
